data.text/html:
Monte Carlo simulation: a time machine made of random numbers

An interactive companion to IBM Technology's "What is Monte Carlo Simulation?" (Martin Keen).
"Monte Carlo simulation is a mathematical technique used to estimate the possible outcomes of an uncertain event. It's a chance to see into the future."
The video answers three questions, and so does this notebook:
  1. How do they work? Random sampling, illustrated with two dice.
  2. Who uses them? Portfolio management, risk analysis, option pricing, capacity planning.
  3. How do you run one? Three steps: model → distributions → simulate repeatedly, then measure the spread.
Color language used throughout: ■ purple = simulated samples / estimates · ■ red = the exact (true) answer · ■ orange = risk, thresholds and "bad" outcomes · ■ teal = "good" outcomes / targets met.

data.text/markdown:
1 · How do they work? Random sampling with two dice

The video's example: what is the probability that two dice sum to 7? Brute force by reasoning: there are ||(6 \times 6 = 36||) equally likely combinations, and 6 of them sum to 7, so ||[P(\text{sum}=7) = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.1667.||]Monte Carlo: forget the counting. Just roll (randomly sample) many times and count: ||[\hat P(\text{sum}=7) = \frac{\#\{\text{rolls that sum to 7}\}}{N}.||]The simulator below rolls the dice in your browser. The purple bars are the observed frequencies, the red ticks are the exact probabilities ||(\tfrac{6-|s-7|}{36}||).

data.text/markdown:
2 · "The more you sample, the more accurate": the ||(1/\sqrt{N}||) law

The video ends with a key rule: "the more you sample, the more accurate your sampling range, and the better your estimation." How much more accurate? An estimate built from ||(N||) independent samples has standard deviation (the standard error) ||[\operatorname{SE}(\hat P) = \sqrt{\frac{P(1-P)}{N}} \;\propto\; \frac{1}{\sqrt N}.||]So 4× more samples only halves the error, and 100× more samples buys one extra decimal digit. Predict first: how many rolls do you need so that the 95 % range of ||(\hat P(7)||) is within ±0.01 of 1/6?
Pick a guess and lock it in to see the answer.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Who uses them? A portfolio you can't predict

"Perhaps the most well-known application is portfolio management and investment planning. By running thousands or even millions of simulations, investors get a better idea of how their portfolio might perform under different market conditions." We'll build exactly that, following the video's three steps to run a Monte Carlo simulation:
Step (video) In our portfolio
1. Set up the predictive model: dependent variable ← independent (input/risk) variables final wealth ||(V_T||) ← yearly returns ||(r_1,\dots,r_T||): ||(\;V_t = V_{t-1}(1+r_t) + c||)
2. Specify the probability distribution of the inputs (historical data or analyst judgment) you paint the distribution of a yearly return ||(r||)
3. Run simulations repeatedly, drawing random inputs each time draw ||(T||) returns, compute ||(V_T||), repeat thousands of times

Step 2 · Paint the distribution of yearly returns

Drag across the bars to paint "probability weights" (the video: assign probability weights to a range of likely values). Presets give you a starting point. The red line is the mean return, the orange band ±1 standard deviation.

Steps 1 & 3 · The model, run thousands of times

Set the rest of the predictive model (start value, yearly contribution ||(c||), horizon ||(T||)) and a goal. Each simulated future draws ||(T||) independent returns from your painted distribution. Purple lines are a few individual futures; the shaded fan shows the 5–95 % and 25–75 % ranges across all of them.

data.text/markdown:
4 · Measure the spread: variance, standard deviation, and "enough" simulations

The video: "you'll also want to compute the range of variation within a sample by calculating the variance and the standard deviation, which are commonly used measures of spread." Two different spreads matter:
formula what it tells you shrinks with more sims?
spread of outcomes ||(s = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{N-1}\sum_i (V^{(i)} - \bar V)^2}||) how uncertain the future is no, it's a property of the world
spread of the estimate ||(\operatorname{SE} = s/\sqrt{N}||) how uncertain your Monte Carlo answer is yes, like ||(1/\sqrt N||)
Drag the slider to use only the first ||(N||) of your portfolio simulations from Section 3.

data.text/markdown:
5 · Sandbox: capacity planning ("planning for spare capacity")

Another application from the video. You run a service and must decide how many servers to provision. Daily demand is uncertain, so build the model with the three steps:
  1. Model: load ||(= \text{users} \times \text{requests per user}||) (+ a rare traffic spike). Overloaded if load ||(>||) capacity.
  2. Distributions: users ~ Normal(μ, σ), requests/user ~ Uniform(a, b), spike ~ Bernoulli(p) × multiplier.
  3. Simulate many days and read off ||(P(\text{overload})||).
Play with the knobs; the challenges below give you targets.
